steps.output_raw:
<think>
</think>
<plan>
1. Reassure the user and confirm they did the right thing shutting off water.
2. Give concise, stepwise guidance for cleanup, drying, and minimizing damage/mold.

4. Clarify I can’t send a real plumber, and advise on who to call and when.
</plan>
<action type="say">
You did the right thing turning that knob off — that’s huge. Since the water is clean tank/line water and it’s stopped, this is now mostly a cleanup and “prevent damage” situation.

Do this next, in order:

1. Protect anything important  
   - Move electronics, books, cardboard boxes, rugs, etc. out of the wet area ASAP.  
   - If water’s hitting the ceiling below, put a bucket/pan under any drips.

2. Get as much water up as possible (hard floor first)  
   - Use towels/old clothes/blankets to soak up standing water on the bathroom floor. Wring them out in the tub/shower and repeat.  
   - If you have a wet/dry Shop-Vac, you can use that (but only if it’s rated for water).

3. Deal with the carpet at the hallway  
   - Lay dry towels on the wet carpet and walk/press on them to pull moisture up. Swap them out as they get soaked.  
   - If you have any fans, point them at the wet carpet and bathroom floor. Keep good airflow (door open, fan running).  
   - If you have a small space heater or dehumidifier, you can use it in the same area (but don’t overheat or leave it unattended).

4. Disinfect the bathroom floor  
   - Once the visible water is up, wipe/mop with a mild cleaner or diluted bleach solution (if safe for your floor type) since it’s still “toilet area” water.  
   - Avoid flooding it again with too much solution; better a damp clean than another mini-flood.

5. Don’t use the toilet until it’s checked  
   - Leave the shutoff valve behind the toilet in the OFF position.  
   - Likely issues: stuck fill valve, broken float, or flapper problem causing it to run and overflow.

6. Contact the right person  
   - If you rent: call/text your landlord or building maintenance and say:  
     “My toilet overflowed from the tank side. I shut off the supply valve. The toilet was flushing weird, then wouldn’t stop filling and overflowed. I need a plumber to check/repair it and I’ve started drying the floor and carpet.”  
   - If you own: call a local plumber and say the same. Ask about urgency; since water is off and clean, this is usually “same day/next-day” urgent, not 911-level.

Watch for these red flags (call a pro ASAP if you see them):  
- Ceiling below starting to bulge, sag, or discolor.  
- Carpet staying squishy-wet for more than a day even with towels/fans.  
- Any weird electrical issues (flickering lights, outlets near the water, etc.).

If you tell me what kind of flooring is in the bathroom (tile, vinyl, wood/laminate) and whether you’re renting or own, I can give more specific “what to do in the next few hours / what to tell the landlord or plumber.”</action>

- Keep soaking up water with towels until:
  - No visible standing water, even in corners/behind the toilet.
  - Grout looks more matte than shiny.  
- After that:
  - Wipe/mop with a cleaner or a small amount of diluted bleach (if your tile can handle it), then dry again with towels.  
- Leave the bathroom door open and, if you have a fan, aim it across the floor toward the doorway.

- Focus where the water crossed from tile to carpet:
  - Lay dry towels over the wet carpet, then step/walk on them to press water out; swap towels as they get soaked.  
  - If possible, gently lift just the very edge of the carpet at the threshold (without ripping it up) so a bit of air can get under there.

- If you or a neighbor has a wet/dry vac or carpet cleaner, use it to suck water out (don’t flood the carpet with extra water).

a) Take photos:  
- The toilet, clearly showing the shutoff valve turned off.  
- The wet bathroom floor.  
- The wet carpet (close-up and from farther away).  
- Any signs of spread (baseboards, lower walls, ceiling under the bathroom if you can see it).

Subject: URGENT – Toilet overflow and water on floor/carpet

“Hi,

Please send maintenance/plumbing as soon as possible to:  
1) Repair the toilet so it is safe to use, and  
2) Inspect and properly dry/clean the affected areas (including under the carpet) to prevent mold or long-term damage.  

I have taken photos of the incident and my cleanup efforts.  
Thank you.”

If there’s an “emergency maintenance” phone number, also call and say the short version out loud, then note the time you called and who you spoke to.

This combo—fast drying + clear paper trail that you reported it right away—goes a long way against mold issues and blame.
